text: The capstone is built. This final lesson is the architecture review every production system should get before being signed off — checking the finished system against the course's own standards, not just confirming it runs.

Run it against Lesson 5's five mistakes. One: simulator-first — the full eighty-iteration loop and injected-failure handling were verified before any real-hardware submission. Two and three: a real retry and fallback decision table, plus a circuit breaker at twelve hundred dollars. Four: every cost value is reported with its standard error, never a bare number. Five: one adapter interface let the project swap between simulator and Rigetti Ankaa-3 without touching orchestration code.

A completed run's ledger should tell a coherent story on its own — this is a real run history from Amazon Braket, the same shape a finished operational log should let a reviewer read without re-running anything.

Here's that story in numbers. Eighty successful iterations, four with one retried failure each, total cost one thousand eight dollars, total wall-clock time around fifty-eight minutes. Every one of those numbers traces to a specific ledger entry — and one open item from kickoff never got resolved: running this daily would cost twenty-one thousand one hundred twenty dollars a month. A genuine second-pass review doesn't let that quietly disappear.
And here's the real control this entire project was built around protecting — Amazon Braket's spending limits, reviewed one final time as part of signing off.

Swap the ansatz and the cost function — a QAOA cut-value, a classifier's loss function — and every other piece of this architecture carries over unchanged: the state machine, the batching strategy, the retry and fallback table, the cost ledger and circuit breaker, the simulator-first testing discipline. That transferability is the actual deliverable of this course. Not a working VQE demo, but a reusable classical orchestration pattern for any hybrid workload you build next.
